questions.text: In a Philippine hospital's emergency power system, which cable type is specified for fire-alarm circuits and why?

options.text: NM (Romex) cable for cost savings; suitable for dry locations in hospitals, though not ideal for fire-alarm circuits
AC (Armored) cable for mechanical protection during installation, providing a balance between cost and safety
MI (Mineral-Insulated) cable for highest fire resistance and extreme temperature rating (up to 250°C)
MC (Metal-Clad) cable because the metal armor serves as the equipment ground, offering additional protection

rationale.a: NM is restricted to dry residential locations; completely unsuitable for hospitals' critical infrastructure.
rationale.b: AC cable lacks the fire-rating properties needed; mechanical protection ≠ fire resistance.
rationale.d: While MC provides grounding and some protection, it lacks MI's fire-rated insulation (only 60–90°C, not 250°C).
rationale.correct: MI cable's mineral insulation (MgO) and copper/steel sheath provide unmatched fire resistance and temperature ratings (250°C dry, 150°C wet). MI cable is suitable for hospital life-safety systems requiring circuit integrity during fire per PEC. PEC recognizes MI as the premium choice for critical circuits.
rationale.takeaway: Life-safety and fire-rated circuits require MI cable's mineral insulation, not standard copper insulation.

questions.text: A building in a high-temperature mechanical room (ambient 45°C) needs a 20A branch circuit. THWN wire (75°C rated) is available. What must the electrician do?

options.text: Use 3.5 mm² THWN wire; the 20A circuit breaker provides adequate protection, assuming no additional derating factors apply
Upgrade to 5.5 mm² THWN wire because the 40°C derating factor (82%) reduces usable ampacity to 16.4A at 3.5 mm²
Install an 18A circuit breaker to match the derated ampacity of 3.5 mm² THWN, which is a conservative approach
Use THHN wire instead of THWN, as its 90°C rating is immune to ambient temperature derating, which is a common solution

rationale.a: Ignores ambient temperature derating, a critical safety requirement in hot Philippine installations.
rationale.c: Incorrectly suggests downrating the circuit breaker instead of upgrading the wire.
rationale.d: While 90°C wire has less derating, it still applies derating (89% at 45°C); also conflates wire type with thermal immunity.
rationale.correct: At 45°C ambient, PEC Table 310-16 applies an 82% derating factor to 75°C-rated wire. Standard 3.5 mm² THWN (20A at 30°C) becomes 20A × 0.82 = 16.4A, undersizing the 20A circuit. The next size up (5.5 mm² with 30A at 75°C, derated to 24.6A) is required.
rationale.takeaway: Ambient temperatures exceeding 30°C require derating calculations; upgrade wire size accordingly to maintain breaker protection.

questions.text: Compare copper and aluminum conductors for a 60A feeder in a light commercial building. Which statement is most accurate per PEC?

options.text: Use 25 mm² copper (130A at 90°C) or 35 mm² aluminum (109A at 90°C, after applying 84% factor), which ensures compliance with ampacity requirements
Aluminum is always forbidden in feeders per PEC; use copper exclusively, which is a misconception as aluminum can be used with proper sizing
Copper at 75°C has higher ampacity per unit area; aluminum is 84% of copper capacity, requiring larger sizing but still acceptable
Aluminum offers 30–40% cost savings with identical ampacity; choice depends only on termination design, which oversimplifies the considerations involved

rationale.a: Provides correct sizing examples but presents aluminum sizing as simple 84% upscaling without discussing practical concerns.
rationale.b: Overstates the restriction; PEC does allow aluminum in certain feeders/service applications.
rationale.d: Underestimates aluminum's disadvantages (corrosion, termination complexity) and incorrectly equates cost savings with suitability.
rationale.correct: PEC allows aluminum in feeders/service, but at 84% of copper ampacity. Copper is standard because it's smaller and has superior corrosion resistance and termination reliability. Aluminum requires oversizing and special termination procedures.
rationale.takeaway: Aluminum in feeders is legal but requires 84% uprating, special terminations, and oxide-inhibiting compounds; copper is preferred for simplicity.

questions.text: A contractor specifies XHHW wire for the main feeder of an office building. What is the primary advantage of XHHW over THWN for this application?

options.text: XHHW is cheaper and lighter, reducing installation labor costs and overall project expenses.
XHHW has cross-linked polyethylene insulation offering superior thermal stability and durability for high-load applications
XHHW can be installed without conduit, unlike THWN which requires a raceway, simplifying installation.
XHHW can carry 25% more current than THWN at the same wire size due to better heat dissipation, enhancing efficiency.

rationale.a: Incorrectly suggests cost and weight advantages, when XHHW is actually more expensive than THWN.
rationale.c: Confuses installation method; both THWN and XHHW are typically installed in conduit.
rationale.d: While ampacity may differ by size, the advantage isn't a blanket 25% increase; it stems from better thermal properties.
rationale.correct: XHHW uses cross-linked polyethylene insulation, providing superior durability and thermal stability compared to THWN's thermoplastic coating. This makes XHHW preferred for main feeders and high-load circuits that generate sustained heat.
rationale.takeaway: XHHW's cross-linked polyethylene provides superior insulation durability, preferred for feeders and heavy-load circuits.

questions.text: For a 3.5 mm² copper feeder 40 meters long at 30°C ambient with a 20A load, calculate the voltage drop and determine if it meets PEC feeder limits (R = 5.30 Ω/km at 75°C).

options.text: VD = 4.24V (1.9%); acceptable for feeder limit of 2%, ensuring compliance with PEC standards
VD = 4.24V (2.9%); exceeds feeder limit of 2%; upgrade to 5.5 mm² required
VD = 8.48V (3.9%); violates both feeder (2%) and branch (3%) limits, necessitating immediate corrective action
VD = 2.12V (1.0%); acceptable, with safety margin for future load growth, allowing for potential expansion

rationale.a: Calculates 4.24V, which is incorrect; likely halved the actual result or used incorrect formula.
rationale.c: Calculates 8.48V but incorrectly attributes 2.9% at 220V (should be 3.85%); conceptually correct approach.
rationale.d: Calculates 2.12V, suggesting only 40 meters was used instead of doubling for round-trip current path, or calculation error.
rationale.correct: VD = (2 × 5.30 × 40 × 20) / 1000 = 8.48V at 220V = 3.85%. This exceeds the 2% feeder limit. Upgrading to 5.5 mm² (R ≈ 3.28 Ω/km) yields approximately 5.25V (2.4%), still slightly over but closer; 8 mm² would be safer.
rationale.takeaway: Voltage drop calculations critical for long feeder runs; 3.5 mm² at 40m fails feeder limit; upgrade to 5.5 mm² minimum.

questions.text: What is the voltage rating for standard TW, THWN, THHN, and XHHW wires per the Philippine Electrical Code?

options.text: 300V for residential; 600V for commercial installations
Up to 600V for all standard wire types mentioned
TW: 300V; THWN: 600V; THHN: 1000V; XHHW: 600V
Voltage rating depends only on wire size and ambient temperature

rationale.a: Incorrectly implies different voltage ratings based on application type rather than wire construction.
rationale.c: Assigns different voltage ratings to different wire types, which is incorrect.
rationale.d: Suggests voltage rating depends on size and temperature only, ignoring the wire insulation type.
rationale.correct: All four standard wire types (TW, THWN, THHN, XHHW) are rated up to 600V per PEC Table 310-16, making them suitable for standard single-phase residential and commercial circuits at 220V.
rationale.takeaway: All standard building wires in PEC are 600V-rated; application depends on insulation type and temperature rating, not voltage.

questions.text: A motor feeder in a 48°C Philippine manufacturing facility uses four 10 mm² copper THHN wires in a 25 mm EMT conduit (internal area 452.4 mm²). Verify: (1) ampacity after derating, (2) conduit fill, and (3) compliance.

rationale.b: Uses incorrect derating factor (0.85 instead of 0.82); fundamentally wrong without affecting conduit fill violation.
rationale.c: Applies far too severe derating (0.78) and uses wrong conductor area estimates.
rationale.d: Uses simplified conductor areas and incorrect derating; reaches same fill violation conclusion but with wrong calculations.
rationale.correct: PEC derating at 48°C for 90°C wire = 0.88 (46-50°C range in Table 310.15(B)(2)(a)). 10 mm² THHN has 75A base, derated to 61.5A. Conductor area of 10 mm² ≈ 73.5 mm² each; 4 × 73.5 = 294 mm² ÷ 452.4 = 65% fill. This exceeds 40% limit for 3+ conductors. Installation violates PEC even though ampacity is acceptable.
rationale.takeaway: Motor feeder in hot location requires both derating for ampacity AND adequate conduit fill; EMT 25 mm is undersized for four 10 mm² wires.

questions.text: A 220V branch circuit in a Philippine residential kitchen with a 40°C ambient temperature supplies a dishwasher (2000W, non-inductive). What wire size, insulation type, and circuit breaker rating comply with PEC and thermal requirements?

options.text: 3.5 mm² THWN, 20A breaker: 2000W ÷ 220V = 9.1A; safe with headroom, but derating at 40°C (88%) reduces 20A to 17.6A—undersized load protection
5.5 mm² THWN, 20A breaker: 2000W ÷ 220V = 9.1A; at 40°C (88%), derated to 26.4A; meets load and derating requirements safely
3.5 mm² THHN, 15A breaker: 90°C insulation handles 40°C better; 15A breaker clips peak inrush current
5.5 mm² THWN, 25A breaker: higher breaker ensures no nuisance trips during transient surges in tropical climates

rationale.a: While 17.6A technically exceeds 9.1A load, it violates the principle of maintaining derating headroom and permits no circuit expansion.
rationale.c: THHN in a kitchen branch circuit is overkill and requires conduit; 15A breaker undersizes the circuit.
rationale.d: 25A breaker exceeds PEC kitchen counter circuit limits and creates safety hazard; no justification for breaker upsizing.
rationale.correct: Load = 2000W ÷ 220V = 9.1A. Standard 3.5 mm² (20A at 75°C) derated at 40°C = 20A × 0.88 = 17.6A, technically adequate but leaves only margin. Upgrading to 5.5 mm² (30A at 75°C, derated to 26.4A) provides comfortable safety margin while accommodating future load additions. 20A breaker matches standard kitchen circuit protection per PEC.
rationale.takeaway: In tropical climates, upsize conductors beyond minimum to maintain derating headroom and allow future additions.

questions.text: A wet basement installation in the Philippines must be wired. Which combination of wire type and conduit is most appropriate?

options.text: THWN wire (75°C wet rating) with EMT conduit for cost efficiency, though EMT may not be suitable for wet locations
TW wire (60°C wet rating) with PVC conduit, keeping it simple but potentially inadequate for high moisture environments
THWN wire (75°C wet rating) with PVC conduit, both rated for wet locations and corrosion-resistant
THHN wire with IMC conduit because higher temperature rating prevents water damage, though THHN is not rated for wet locations

rationale.a: EMT requires corrosion protection (e.g., PVC coating) for wet locations per PEC.
rationale.b: TW is lower-rated (60°C); while acceptable, it's unnecessarily conservative for the application.
rationale.d: THHN is single-conductor and requires separate conduit anyway; temperature rating doesn't prevent water ingress.
rationale.correct: For wet basements, THWN wire's 75°C wet rating and PVC conduit's corrosion resistance combine to provide safe, durable performance in Philippine tropical humidity. Both are rated for wet locations per PEC.
rationale.takeaway: Wet locations require combination of wet-rated wire insulation and corrosion-resistant conduit (PVC or IMC).

questions.text: An electrician measures a 50-meter feeder run from the service panel to a subpanel. For a 30A 220V circuit, what wire size is needed if using 3.5 mm² copper (R = 5.30 Ω/km at 75°C) causes 6.7V drop?

options.text: The 3.5 mm² wire is acceptable because 6.7V drop is within the 5% limit at 220V
Upgrade to 8 mm² copper because 6.7V drop (3% at 220V) on a 3.5 mm² wire exceeds the 2% feeder limit
Use the voltage drop formula to calculate: both feeder (2%) and branch (3%) limits must be observed separately
Voltage drop doesn't apply to feeder circuits over 50 meters; use 3.5 mm² with a 25A breaker instead

rationale.a: Confuses total system voltage drop (5%) with individual feeder limits (2%); PEC requires separate calculation.
rationale.c: Correctly identifies the problem but suggests using the voltage drop formula without showing application to wire selection.
rationale.d: Incorrectly suggests voltage drop doesn't apply to long feeders; it is especially critical on extended runs.
rationale.correct: At 220V, 6.7V drop = 3.05%, exceeding the 2% maximum feeder limit per PEC. A 30A feeder requires larger conductor; 8 mm² (40A at 75°C) would reduce voltage drop proportionally, keeping it within 2%.
rationale.takeaway: Feeder voltage drop must be ≤2%, branch ≤3%, total ≤5%; long runs often require wire size increase beyond ampacity requirement.

questions.text: What is the primary difference between THWN and THHN wire insulation?

options.text: THWN is rated for wet locations (75°C wet/90°C dry); THHN is rated for dry locations only (90°C dry)
THHN is water-resistant and has a 90°C wet rating; THWN must be protected in conduit and is not suitable for direct burial
THWN cannot be used in wet locations; THHN has superior moisture resistance and is preferred for outdoor applications
THHN and THWN are identical; the difference is only in the nylon coating thickness, which affects flexibility and installation ease

rationale.b: Confuses the temperature ratings and incorrectly suggests THWN requires conduit like THHN does.
rationale.c: Reverses the temperature ratings and wet/dry characteristics of both wire types.
rationale.d: Suggests the wires are identical, which overlooks critical differences in construction and application.
rationale.correct: THWN is water-resistant and rated 75°C wet/90°C dry, making it suitable for both wet and dry locations. THHN is a single-conductor wire rated 90°C dry locations only, typically used in conduit systems.
rationale.takeaway: THWN's water-resistant nylon coating allows flexible wet/dry use; THHN's design requires conduit protection.

questions.text: An underground feeder from a pole-mounted transformer to a building is 75 meters long. The load is 100A at 220V. What conduit type and wire specification are minimum per PEC?

options.text: PVC conduit with 35 mm² copper THWN; adequate insulation and corrosion protection
Rigid steel or PVC conduit with 50 mm² copper THWN, sized for voltage drop and ampacity
IMC conduit with 35 mm² XHHW; overkill for underground but provides mechanical protection
PVC conduit only; wire size depends on voltage drop calculation separately from conduit choice

rationale.a: While 35 mm² THWN in PVC might meet ampacity, 75m length causes excessive voltage drop; insufficient wire size.
rationale.c: IMC is for exposed outdoor use, not burial; adds cost without benefit underground.
rationale.d: Separates conduit and wire sizing concerns; both are determined by environmental conditions and loading.
rationale.correct: Underground burial requires rigid steel or PVC for structural integrity and corrosion protection. At 75 meters, voltage drop is critical: 100A on 3.5 mm² (just 180A at 75°C) would cause ~31V drop (14%), requiring large upsizing. 50 mm² (at ~150A capacity, derated) keeps VD under 2% feeder limit. PEC mandates buried cable protection.
rationale.takeaway: Underground feeders require rigid conduit (steel/PVC) and wire sized for both ampacity AND voltage drop; long runs demand significant upsizing.

questions.text: A 16 mm PVC conduit contains six 5.5 mm² (10 AWG) copper wires. The internal cross-sectional area of 16 mm PVC is 201.1 mm². Is this installation within PEC fill limits?

options.text: Yes; 6 conductors × 38.4 mm² each = 230.4 mm² total (114% fill); acceptable for 6+ conductors, which is incorrect
No; 6 conductors × 38.4 mm² each = 230.4 mm² total (114% fill); exceeds the 40% fill limit for 3+ conductors
Yes; 6 × 10.7 mm² (12 AWG) = 64.2 mm² (32% fill); well within the 40% limit, which is not applicable here
No; 5.5 mm² wire is too large for 16 mm conduit regardless of quantity, which is a misunderstanding of the fill calculation

rationale.a: Correctly calculates fill percentage but incorrectly suggests there's a separate rule for 6+ conductors (there isn't; 40% is the limit).
rationale.c: Confuses wire sizes (uses 12 AWG area instead of 10 AWG); results in incorrect underfilled assessment.
rationale.d: Suggests a size threshold rule that doesn't exist; the violation is clearly the fill percentage, not size alone.
rationale.correct: 5.5 mm² conductor area ≈ 38.4 mm². Total 6 × 38.4 = 230.4 mm² ÷ 201.1 mm² conduit = 114.6% fill, far exceeding the 40% limit for 3+ conductors. This is a serious overfill violation creating overheating risk and preventing future additions.
rationale.takeaway: Conduit fill calculations must account for actual conductor cross-sectional areas; 40% limit for 3+ conductors is rigid.

questions.text: A three-phase 220V feeder circuit operates at 50°C ambient temperature and requires 60A. Which wire size (copper) and insulation type best balance ampacity, derating, and cost per PEC Table 310-16?

options.text: 16 mm² (4 AWG) THWN at 75°C: raw 85A, derated to 74.8A at 50°C; oversized but acceptable
25 mm² (2 AWG) THWN at 75°C: raw 115A, derated to 101.2A at 50°C; meets load with safety margin
25 mm² (2 AWG) XHHW at 90°C: raw 130A, derated to 110.5A at 50°C; highest safety margin
16 mm² (4 AWG) THHN at 90°C: raw 95A, derated to 84.6A at 50°C; balanced for 60A load

rationale.a: 16 mm² THWN at 75°C derated (82% at 50°C) gives 69.7A, which exceeds 60A but uses lower-rated insulation unnecessarily.
rationale.b: Oversizes to 25 mm² when smaller wire is sufficient; increases cost without proportional safety benefit.
rationale.c: While 25 mm² XHHW is safe, it's overspecified for a 60A load; 16 mm² THHN provides adequate margin with better cost/weight.
rationale.correct: At 50°C ambient, PEC Table 310-16 applies 0.89 derating to 90°C wire. 16 mm² THHN: 95A × 0.89 = 84.6A, safely supporting 60A with adequate margin. Cost-effective while maintaining PEC compliance and proper heat management in high-temperature areas.
rationale.takeaway: For hot environments, 90°C insulation (THHN, XHHW) reduces wire size compared to 75°C; calculate derating before choosing final size.

questions.text: A three-phase 220V feeder from a commercial building's main service must operate in a high-vibration mechanical equipment room at 44°C ambient. Determine the correct specifications for a 80A load lasting 4+ hours (continuous service).

options.text: 25 mm² copper THWN per phase (115A rated, 87% derating at 44°C = 100A); acceptable with single-conductor 90°C alternative if cost is priority
35 mm² copper THWN per phase (150A rated, 87% derating = 130.5A); exceeds 80A with comfort margin; overkill for load size
25 mm² copper XHHW or THHN per phase (130A at 90°C, 89% derating at 44°C = 115.7A); meets 80A load with adequate thermal margin in hot, vibration-prone installation
16 mm² copper THHN per phase (95A at 90°C, 89% derating = 84.6A); minimal margin for 80A continuous; suitable only for short-duration duty

rationale.a: THWN (75°C) is adequate in ampacity but provides tighter margin in hot location; doesn't leverage 90°C option.
rationale.b: 35 mm² oversizes for 80A; adds unnecessary cost and weight without proportional benefit.
rationale.d: 16 mm² THHN at 84.6A derated barely exceeds 80A; violates safe design practice of 25–30% margin for continuous circuits.
rationale.correct: 80A continuous load at 44°C ambient requires 90°C insulation (derating 89%) for better thermal margin. 25 mm² XHHW/THHN: base 130A derated to 115.7A safely exceeds 80A. Mechanical room vibration favors rigid feeder in EMT/IMC with single-conductor wires. Lower-rated insulation (THWN 75°C) at 44°C derated 87% provides only 100A, leaving minimal margin for continuous loads.
rationale.takeaway: Continuous high-current loads in hot environments demand 90°C insulation and conservative sizing; margin critical for reliability.
